content.title: About
content.content: Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera) are small, leaf-budgeted buds resembling miniature cabbages. They belong to the Gemmifera cultivar group of cabbages and are native to the region around Brussels, Belgium, where they gained popularity in the 16th century. Roasted, steamed, or sautéed, they have a nutty, earthy flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brussels sprouts grow on thick, long stalks in spiraling clusters.
Selective breeding in recent decades has significantly reduced their bitter taste.
They belong to the same species as broccoli, cabbage, and kale.
High heat roasting caramelizes their natural sugars, transforming their flavor profile.
They are extremely popular as a traditional holiday side dish.

items.title: Rich in Vitamin K
items.content: Essential for blood clotting and bone health maintenance.

items.title: High Antioxidant Content
items.content: Contains kaempferol, an antioxidant that helps reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Excellent Fiber Source
items.content: Supports regular gut motility and blood sugar stability.

items.title: Contains Omega-3 Fatty Acids
items.content: One of the few plant sources containing ALA omega-3 fats.

items.title: Immune Boosting
items.content: Provides over 100% of the daily recommended value of vitamin C per cup.

items.title: Vitamin K and Blood Thinners
items.content: People on blood thinners like Warfarin should maintain consistent vitamin K intake.

items.title: Digestive Upset
items.content: May cause gas or bloating due to complex carbohydrates like raffinose.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Trim stems, halve them, and roast at high heat with olive oil, salt, and pepper. You can also shred them raw into winter salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh sprouts unwashed in a plastic bag in the refrigerator for up to a week. Sprouts attached to the stalk last longer.
